meaning: Son of the sea (from Old Irish Manannán)

phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial nasal [m], as in English 'man'.
Short open front [a], the first unstressed syllable.
Alveolar nasal [n], short open front [a], and another [n]; the second syllable carries stress.
Long open front [aː] marked by acute, ending in alveolar nasal [n].

pronunciation.approximation: 'muh-NAH-nawn' — stress the middle syllable, keep the first 'a' short, and lengthen the stressed 'ah' before the final 'n'. The double n hints at a slender or velarized quality in medieval Irish.

pronunciation.note: Manannán is Tier 1: the acute on á is a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses. The double n reflects the Old Irish spelling; the name is traditionally explained as 'son of the sea' (mac Lir).

domains.title: Lord of the Sea and Mist
domains.subtitle: Guardian of the Irish Otherworld
domains.lead: Manannán mac Lir is the great sea god of Ireland and guardian of the Otherworld. He rules the waves, the weather, and the mist that separates the mortal island from the Land of Promise. A shape-shifter, navigator, and bestower of marvelous weapons, he appears in myth as helper, host, and boundary-keeper between this world and the next.

cards.name: Sea Lord
cards.desc: He commands the waters around Ireland and the weather that governs them.

cards.name: Otherworld Guardian
cards.desc: The mist that hides Tír na nÓg and the Isles of the Blessed is his cloak.

cards.name: Treasure-Giver
cards.desc: He bestows weapons, cloaks, and horses on heroes who cross his path.

cards.name: Shape-Shifter
cards.desc: He moves between forms — rider, fisherman, beggar — to test or aid mortals.

mythology.lead: Manannán moves through Irish myth like the tide: now distant, now suddenly present, always connected to the boundary between worlds. He is not a creator or a warrior king but a guardian of passages — between islands, between life and death, between the known and the hidden.

myths.title: The Voyage of Bran
myths.text: In Immram Brain maic Febail, Manannán appears to Bran as he sails toward the Otherworld. From the god's perspective, the sea is a plain of flowers and the ships are chariots. He sings of the blessed lands beyond the wave and urges Bran onward. The poem makes him the poet of the threshold, the one who explains what mortals cannot yet see.

myths.title: The Shrouded Island
myths.text: The Lebor Gabála Érenn ('Book of Invasions') describes Manannán as the one who raises a mist around the island of Tír Tairngire so that it cannot be found. He also governs the weather and the harvest, pouring silver showers on the fields. Here he is less a sea god in the maritime sense than a deity of the invisible boundary between Ireland and the Otherworld.

myths.title: Foster-Father of the Gods
myths.text: In the late tale Altram Tige Dá Medar, Manannán acts as foster-father to the children of the gods, including the Dagda's son Angus. He provides the sídhe mounds where the divine race dwells after mortal Ireland is given to human invaders. The story expands his role from sea guardian to provider of the Otherworld's real estate.

lore.syncretism: Manannán's closest counterpart is the Welsh Manawydan fab Llŷr, who appears in the Second and Third Branches of the Mabinogi as a patient, just, and sea-associated figure married to the goddess Rhiannon. Both names derive from a Common Celtic *Manaw- and share the element 'son of Lir/Llŷr' (sea). Some scholars have compared Manannán to the Romano-Celtic sea god Manannus and to broader Celtic maritime deities such as the Gaulish Lugus or the syncretic Neptune. In the Isle of Man, the figure survived into folk tradition as Mannan beg mac y Leir, and his name is preserved in the island's name itself. Christian scribes euhemerized him as an ancient sea-king.
lore.culturalLegacy: Manannán left his name on the Isle of Man and on countless coastal places around Ireland. In modern Irish and Manx folklore he persists as a guardian of the sea, sometimes as a Christianized saint, sometimes as an undying pagan lord. Contemporary Celtic-inspired fantasy, Neopaganism, and Irish-language literature revive him as a god of mists, voyages, and the hidden world just beyond the shore. For island peoples, he remains the deity who makes sense of the sea: not merely a barrier, but a road to somewhere else.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Manannán is the god of the horizon. He does not rule the land; he rules the mist that hides the land beyond the land. His gifts — the boat that needs no oars, the horse that runs on water, the sword that cannot be refused — are all instruments of passage.

To meet Manannán is to discover that the boundary you thought was an end is actually a door. The sea that separates Ireland from Tír na nÓg is the same sea that brings the fog, the fish, and the stranger. He asks us to become navigators of uncertainty: to trust the invisible road, to accept the cloak of mist, and to remember that every shore is someone else's threshold.

lore.archaeology: No inscription names Manannán directly, but the material culture of Irish seafaring — currachs, coastal promontory forts, and votive deposits in rivers and bogs — provides the context for his cult. The Isle of Man's name and tradition of Manannán as a protective sea-lord suggest a long regional memory. Romano-Celtic inscriptions to sea deities and the Gaulish god Manannus may reflect related maritime divinities, though none can be securely identified with the Irish god.
